label: Bonus Section

items: Branch = safe parallel workspace; main = the real version
Merge = bringing a branch's changes into main after review
README = the project's front door; read it first
artifact.label: Reference
artifact.title: GitHub mental model

commonMistakes: Treating GitHub like a file share; the history and review trail are the point.
Editing the main branch directly in the web UI when a change should go through a branch and pull request.
Judging a project by its file list instead of its README, recent commits, and release notes.

coreConcepts.text: A repo holds a project's files plus their complete history. Unlike a shared drive, every change is recorded with who made it, when, and why — and any earlier state can be recovered.
coreConcepts.title: A Repository Is A Project With A Memory

coreConcepts.text: A commit is one recorded change with a message explaining it. A project's history is a chain of commits, which is why engineers can answer 'when did this change, and who approved it' precisely.
coreConcepts.title: Commits Are The Units Of Change

coreConcepts.text: Work happens on a branch — a parallel copy of the project — so unfinished or risky changes never touch the main version until they are reviewed and merged. The main branch is the version everyone treats as real.
coreConcepts.title: Branches Make Change Safe

coreConcepts.text: A clone is your local working copy. A fork is your own server-side copy of someone else's repo, used to propose changes when you do not have direct write access.
coreConcepts.title: Forks And Clones Are Copies With Different Jobs

steps: Scan the commit list and read the messages, not the code.
Open a merged pull request and find who approved it.
doThisNow.task: Open a GitHub repo you have been linked to before and find: the README, the three most recent commits, and one merged pull request.

lessons.objective: Explain what a repository is, what a commit records, and why branches exist.

resources.note: GitHub's own plain-language introduction to repositories, branches, and pull requests.
resources.title: GitHub Docs — Get started

roleVariants.analyst: Commit history and release notes are a reliable changelog for 'what changed and when' questions.
roleVariants.manager: Ask for the pull request link, not a summary deck; the PR shows scope, discussion, and approval in one place.
roleVariants.operator: If a process depends on a repo, watch its releases; that is where breaking changes are announced.
roleVariants.writer: Documentation lives in repos too — your edits follow the same branch-and-review path as code.

lessons.sequenceRationale: The section opens with the mental model — what GitHub stores and how changes move — before looking at daily engineering habits.

Terminology follows GitHub's own usage: repository, commit, branch, fork, clone, merge.
lessons.subtitle: Repositories, commits, branches, and forks: the version-control layer under modern software.
lessons.title: How GitHub Works
lessons.useWhen: Use this when an engineer sends you a GitHub link and you need to know what you are looking at.
lessons.whyItMatters: GitHub is where engineering work is proposed, reviewed, and shipped — including, increasingly, changes drafted by AI agents. If you can read a repository and a pull request, you can follow (and influence) work that used to be invisible until release day.

workedExample.approach: Open the repo: the README tells you what the project is, the commit list shows the fix with its message and author, and the merged pull request shows the discussion and approval behind it.
workedExample.result: You verified the claim in two minutes, without asking for a status meeting.
workedExample.scenario: An engineer links you to a repo and says 'the fix is in, it merged this morning.'
workedExample.verification: Check the commit date and the merged pull request rather than relying on the message alone — the repo is the source of truth.

commonMistakes: Asking for status in chat when the PR already shows exactly what is blocked.
Treating a green check as proof the change is right; checks test what they are told to test.
Assuming merged means live; deployment and release are separate steps.

coreConcepts.text: Bugs, requests, and tasks are filed as issues: a title, a description, discussion, labels, and an owner. An issue is where 'what and why' is debated before anyone builds.
coreConcepts.title: Issues Are The Work Queue

coreConcepts.text: A pull request (PR) proposes merging a branch into main. It shows the exact diff — what changed, line by line — plus discussion, approvals, and the checks that ran. On a healthy team, nothing reaches main without passing this gate.
coreConcepts.title: Pull Requests Are The Review Gate

coreConcepts.text: CI (continuous integration, usually GitHub Actions) runs tests and builds on every PR. A red check means the change broke something or failed a standard; a green check means it is ready for human review, not that it is correct.
coreConcepts.title: Automated Checks Run Before Humans Decide

coreConcepts.text: Teams package merged work into releases with notes describing what changed. Release notes are the fastest reliable answer to 'what is new in the version we run.'
coreConcepts.title: Releases Are The Shipped Record

coreConcepts.text: Coding agents and bots open pull requests, respond to issues, and run on schedules — xAI's Grok Bot, for example, can be triggered by GitHub activity. The review gate matters more, not less, when some authors are machines.
coreConcepts.title: Agents Now Work Inside This Loop

steps: Start from a release note and pick one item.
Find the merged PR behind it.
Read the review discussion and the checks that ran.
Note where the longest wait was.
doThisNow.task: Trace one real change end to end: find an issue, its pull request, the check results, and the release that shipped it.

lessons.objective: Describe the path a change takes from an idea to a shipped release, and what each gate protects.

roleVariants.analyst: Issue labels and milestones are structured data — they beat anecdotes for 'what is the team working on.'
roleVariants.manager: Your dashboard is the PR list: age, blockers, and who is being waited on are all visible without a status meeting.
roleVariants.operator: When something breaks, the fastest question is 'what merged most recently' — the commit and PR history answers it.
roleVariants.writer: Review the diff view for docs and copy changes; comment on the exact lines you mean.

lessons.sequenceRationale: With the mental model in place, this lesson walks the daily loop: issue, branch, pull request, review, checks, merge, release.

lessons.subtitle: Issues, pull requests, code review, automated checks, and releases — the daily loop, translated.
lessons.title: How Engineers Use GitHub Every Day
lessons.useWhen: Use this when you are waiting on an engineering change and want to see where it actually is in the pipeline.
lessons.whyItMatters: Most 'why is this taking so long' friction is really 'which gate is this change sitting at.' The loop is visible on GitHub if you know where to look: an issue for the what, a pull request for the how, checks for the machine verdict, review for the human one, and a release for the shipped record.

workedExample.approach: Find the issue: is it labeled, assigned, and linked to a PR? Open the PR: are checks green, is a reviewer requested, is anyone waiting on you?
workedExample.result: The PR has been waiting two days on a product review — which is you. You approve the wording in the PR and it merges that afternoon.
workedExample.scenario: You requested a small change three days ago and have heard nothing.
workedExample.verification: Confirm the change shipped by finding it in the next release notes, not by assuming merge means deployed.

items: Problem: what is wrong, in one or two sentences
Impact: who hits it and how often
Done means: the observable end state
Out of scope: anything explicitly not requested
artifact.label: Template
artifact.title: Issue that gets acted on

commonMistakes: Filing a solution ('change the button color') instead of the problem, which hides the real need.
Reviewing everything or nothing; name the parts you checked and the parts you did not.
Giving feedback in a side channel, then being surprised the shipped change missed it.

coreConcepts.text: State the problem, who it affects, what 'done' looks like, and the evidence (links, screenshots, examples). Separate the problem from your proposed solution so the team can solve the right thing.
coreConcepts.title: A Good Issue Is A Decision-Ready Brief

coreConcepts.text: You may not review code, but you can review user-facing copy, docs, behavior against requirements, and whether the change matches the issue. Approving what you checked — and naming what you did not — is genuinely useful signal.
coreConcepts.title: Review What You Own

coreConcepts.text: Feedback inside the issue or PR stays attached to the change and its history. Feedback in chat or email evaporates, and forces the engineer to reconcile two records.
coreConcepts.title: Comment Where The Work Is

coreConcepts.text: Ask an AI assistant to summarize a PR diff, explain an error, or draft an issue from your notes. Verify against the source before posting — you are responsible for what you file under your name.
coreConcepts.title: Use AI As Your Translator

steps: Write the problem without proposing the fix.
Add impact and one piece of evidence.
Send it through the team's normal channel — or file it, if you have access.
doThisNow.task: Rewrite one real request you have pending with engineering as a GitHub-ready issue using the template.

lessons.objective: Contribute to GitHub-based work with well-formed issues, useful reviews, and clear feedback.

resources.note: Hands-on courses (Introduction to GitHub, Review Pull Requests) that take under an hour each.
resources.title: GitHub Skills

roleVariants.analyst: File data requests as issues with the exact fields, filters, and a sample of the expected output.
roleVariants.manager: Your highest-leverage GitHub habit is unblocking: watch for PRs waiting on product or business review and clear them daily.
roleVariants.operator: When you spot a production problem, file the issue with timestamps and evidence before the trail goes cold.
roleVariants.writer: Treat docs and in-product copy PRs as your review queue; they are where your expertise is the gate.

AI-assist guidance follows this program's standing rule: draft with AI, verify against the source, post under your own name.
lessons.subtitle: File issues engineers can act on, review what you are qualified to review, and use AI to keep up.
lessons.title: Working With Engineers On GitHub
lessons.useWhen: Use this when you need something from an engineering team, or when you are asked to review a change.
lessons.whyItMatters: Engineers act fastest on inputs that arrive in the shape the system understands: a clear issue beats a hallway request, and a line-specific PR comment beats a vague 'this feels off' in a meeting a week later.

workedExample.approach: File an issue with the current text, the correct name, where the email is sent from, and a screenshot. When the PR appears, review the diff for the copy and approve the wording.
workedExample.result: The fix merges the same day, with your approval recorded as the product check.
workedExample.scenario: You need the onboarding email fixed: it references a retired product name.
workedExample.verification: After release, trigger the email once and confirm the new text is what actually ships.
